Mars Hermes Pathfinder is a mission-planning prototype developed by HermesX to help future astronauts explore Mars. It integrates NASA and USGS imagery, measured elevation, geological context, thermal observations, and atmospheric reanalysis into a layered navigation interface.

The system balances terrain, travel time, sunlight, scientific priorities, and user-defined resource limits to identify relatively optimal routes among evaluated alternatives. Users can connect science targets and waypoints, estimate mission requirements, check return reserves, and preview journeys through elevation profiles, 3D terrain, and first-person playback.

Designed around Mars’s limited resources and connectivity, the prototype combines a streamlined interface with offline mission packages. It turns complex planetary data into understandable planning information while clearly showing data limitations and modeling assumptions. This helps exploration teams identify potential risks, use finite mission resources more effectively, and accomplish more meaningful science.
details:
Mars Hermes Pathfinder is a Mars exploration mission-planning prototype developed by HermesX. It helps future astronauts select scientifically valuable destinations, compare routes, and prepare expeditions within limited time and resources.

The system integrates NASA and USGS imagery, measured elevation, thermal observations, geological context, and OpenMARS atmospheric reanalysis. Users can explore an online Mars atlas or access detailed local mission areas, including 1-meter elevation grids at Hawksbill Gap and Neretva Vallis. Science targets link directly to NASA/PDS evidence.

Using A-based pathfinding*, the planner balances terrain, travel time, sunlight, scientific priorities, and user-defined resource limits. It identifies relatively optimal routes among evaluated alternatives, supports ordered waypoints and observation stops, estimates mission requirements, and checks return reserves. Optional models assess oxygen, battery, water, and payload assumptions. When conditions exceed limits, the interface explains the relevant constraints.

Users can rehearse journeys through elevation profiles, linked environmental curves, 3D terrain, and first-person playback. Field records, resource updates, and replanning support changing mission conditions, while offline packages preserve saved maps and task information.

Development uses Python, NumPy, Rasterio, and PyProj for data preparation, and JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Canvas, Three.js, and Web Workers for browser-based planning and visualization. Early prototypes used Streamlit and Plotly. GitHub and GitHub Actions support collaboration and automated testing.

The project’s innovation is its integration of scientific target selection, route optimization, resource assessment, and navigation rehearsal. Forward planning answers what available resources can achieve; reverse estimation identifies what a chosen mission requires. Our team prioritized simple operation, robustness, return margins, limited connectivity, and transparent data quality. Historical observations and modeling assumptions remain clearly labeled, and positioning is simulated. The intended impact is better-informed planning that helps exploration teams identify potential risks and accomplish more science with finite resources.
